Over the last year we had demand for a clinical summarization and coding assistant, you know things like discharge summaries and problem list extraction, and we were using a mix of hosted APIs and some on-prem models but it was inconsistent. Latency was a big pain, and cost was eating into margins.
[01:20] Alex Chen: Got it. And when you evaluated options, what made Redwood stand out?
[01:28] Maya Ortiz: The big things were predictable latency and the private deployment options — we needed VPC and KMS integration for PHI. Also the Redwood Console dashboards made it easy to show cost per request to the business folks.
[01:42] Dr. Leo Park: From an engineering side, the serving runtime was attractive. We already had a GPU cluster, and Redwood's Dedicated offering maps well to reserving capacity for nightly batch jobs plus low-latency inference during the day. The KV cache stuff — I think you call it prefix caching? — that shaved a lot of token time off.
[02:05] Alex Chen: Yeah, we call it prefix/KV cache. Did you run a POC? How did that go?
[02:12] Dr. Leo Park: We did a two-week poc. The SE team from Redwood — shoutout to our SE, they were great — helped set up a private deployment in our dev VPC. We ran a benchmark: before Redwood, our average latency for a 1.2k token summary was around 1.8s median on our prior stack, with Redwood Dedicated we got that down to ~650ms median and throughput improved three X for batch workloads.
[02:41] Sam Bennett: And the cost per 1k tokens dropped by about 40% when we tuned batching and quantization profiles. We were surprised by how much the quantized kernels helped on our A100s.
[02:55] Alex Chen: Nice, that's a big delta. Were there any surprises or hiccups during migration?
[03:02] Dr. Leo Park: A few. Our data pipeline had some assumptions about tokenization that caused edge cases, and there were some mislabelled entity issues in early runs. Redwood's team helped instrument tracing so we could see token-level cost and latency, which made troubleshooting faster.
[03:20] Maya Ortiz: For compliance, the SSO/SAML setup and KMS integration took a day or two longer than expected because of our internal change control, but Redwood's security docs — the SOC2 stuff — were comprehensive and helped the legal team sign off.
[03:36] Alex Chen: Great to hear. Can you share concrete business outcomes?
[03:40] Sam Bennett: Sure. For our pilot cohort (about 20 hospitals), we reduced average doctor turnaround time on discharge summaries by roughly 18%, which translated to measurable time savings and reduced billing follow-ups. On the financial side, our token unit cost dropped ~40% which helped justify expanding the feature.
[04:02] Maya Ortiz: Also worth calling out — the Redwood Console's per-route dashboards let product managers own the cost story. We tied quality regressions to prompt sets and saw early alerts when a model update affected extract performance. That saved us a regression incident.
[04:20] Alex Chen: Were you using any fallbacks or multi-model routing?
[04:24] Dr. Leo Park: Yes, we used routing policies to send sensitive PHI inference to the private cluster and non-PHI to a cheaper hosted variant for prototyping. The automatic fallback when the private pool was saturated was handy — requests converted to a compatible quantized variant with slightly higher latency but kept the service up.
[04:44] Alex Chen: That's one of the resiliency patterns we advocate. Any feedback on the developer experience?
[04:50] Sam Bennett: The SDKs were solid. The one friction was some model naming and doc typos — small but we logged them. Overall the onboarding was faster than we expected.
[05:02] Maya Ortiz: For marketing, the case study numbers were compelling — we can show both time savings and unit economics.
[05:08] Alex Chen: Awesome. Quick aside for listeners — can you share a short customer story? Maybe a specific hospital use-case that resonated?
[05:16] Maya Ortiz: Yeah, there was a rural hospital that had limited staff; they used the summarization assistant to triage discharge notes. Nurses reported being able to close cases faster and physicians could focus attention more effectively. It was an emotional win for us.
[05:30] Dr. Leo Park: Tech detail — we had to optimize for smaller GPUs at that site, so Redwood's quantization recommendations were crucial.
[05:40] Alex Chen: Nice. Any concerns about vendor lock-in or portability?
[05:45] Dr. Leo Park: We thought about it. Redwood's model catalog and versioning made it easy to pin model versions, and the abstraction layer meant we could swap the underlying model if needed. There's always some integration work, but the cost/latency benefits justified it.
[06:02] Alex Chen: Good. Listeners often ask about security posture — you mentioned SOC2 and KMS. Anything else to add?
[06:09] Maya Ortiz: Audit logs were important for our compliance team — the console's event logs and the ability to stream audit events to our SIEM closed a big check box. Also the ability to restrict training/data retention was key.
[06:22] Alex Chen: Perfect. Switching gears — how does this story fit into BrightWave's go-to-market?
[06:28] Maya Ortiz: We're packaging the assistant as an add-on to our core analytics suite. It helps with sales conversations to show hard numbers — the 18% turnaround improvement and lower cost per request — and it's driven renewals in our pilot accounts.
[06:40] Sam Bennett: The product roadmap includes more clinical AI features, and Redwood's support for multiple models/quant profiles helps us experiment quickly.
[06:48] Alex Chen: Before we wrap, any quick advice for engineering teams planning a similar migration?
[06:54] Dr. Leo Park: Start with a small POC, focus on tokenization/edge cases, and instrument token-level tracing from day one. Also test quantization profiles early.
[07:06] Maya Ortiz: From PM/marketing side — track both time savings and cost per use, those are the two metrics execs care about.
[07:14] Alex Chen: Great. Okay we'll do a few more quick rapid-fire questions for the podcast. First — favorite unexpected win from the project?
[07:21] Sam Bennett: The nurses' anecdote — seeing actual time saved was unexpectedly powerful.
[07:26] Maya Ortiz: For me, the visibility into token economics — it changed how we price the addon.
[07:32] Alex Chen: And a closing thought — anything you'd tell another health-tech founder considering Redwood?
[07:38] Maya Ortiz: If you care about predictable latency and compliance, Redwood is worth evaluating. The Dedicated/private path gave us the control we needed without building everything ourselves.
[07:50] Dr. Leo Park: I'd add — run performance benchmarks tied to your actual token distributions, not synthetic tests.
[07:58] Alex Chen: Lovely. Okay, we'll wrap up — thanks so much for joining, BrightWave. We'll send the release + transcript and a rough cut of the audio. Anything else?
[08:07] Maya Ortiz: No, thanks Alex. Looking forward to the case study.
